lessons.title: The Quarterback's Process
lessons.blurb: Progressions, hots, sight adjusts and checks.

steps.title: Progressions
steps.body: Each play has an order of reads: the hot if there's a blitz, then the first read, second, third, and finally a checkdown to the back. The coverage decides which side he starts on.

steps.title: Option routes
steps.body: Some receivers choose their route after the snap: against man, break away from the defender's leverage; against zone, settle in the open window between defenders.

steps.title: Checks and kills
steps.body: At the line the quarterback can check to a better play, or 'kill' to the second of two plays called in the huddle, based on the look.

steps.prompt: Put a standard dropback progression in order.
steps.explanation: Beat the blitz first, then work the progression, and take the checkdown when nothing else is open.

steps.prompt: On an option route against zone, what does the receiver do?
steps.explanation: Against zone, find the space between defenders and sit down.

steps.prompt: On an option route against man with inside leverage, where does the receiver break?
steps.explanation: Break away from leverage: the defender is inside, so go outside.

steps.statement: A 'kill' call switches to the second of two plays called in the huddle.
steps.explanation: It lets the quarterback pick the better play once he sees the defense.

steps.title: Catches and tackles
steps.body: An NFL catch needs two feet down in bounds; college needs one. In college a ball carrier is down when a knee touches; in the NFL he's down only if a defender touched him.

steps.title: Hashes and flags
steps.body: NFL hash marks are much closer together, so there's less difference between the wide and short sides of the field. Defensive pass interference is a spot foul in the NFL; in college it's at most 15 yards.

steps.prompt: A receiver catches the ball with one foot in bounds. Catch in the NFL?
choices: No, the NFL needs two feet
steps.explanation: Two feet in bounds in the NFL; one is enough in college.

steps.prompt: A ball carrier slips and his knee hits the ground with nobody touching him. In the NFL, is he down?
choices: No, he can get up and keep running
steps.explanation: In the NFL he must be touched down by a defender. In college the knee down ends it.

steps.statement: College defensive pass interference can be worth more than 15 yards.
steps.explanation: College DPI is capped at 15 yards; the NFL spots it where the foul happened.
